text_a: This section is intended for full service clients that issue Visa cards. These issuers have special processing considerations, which this section describes. Visa POS Issuers Visa POS acquirers can choose to send transactions using the full service or the authorization- only processing method. The authorization-only acquirer sends above-floor-limit POS transactions made with a Visa POS card as authorization requests (0100s). One to several days later, the acquirer submits BASE II clearing records (TC 05s and TC 06s). V.I.P. clears these BASE II records to full service issuers as deferred clearing advices (0220s), messages similar to the online deferred clearing advices. As a result, Visa POS issuers that choose to process transactions using the full service method must be prepared to receive online financial transactions from full service acquirers, and to receive authorization messages followed by deferred clearing transactions from full service and authorization-only acquirers. For authorization-only acquired POS transactions, the full service issuer must be prepared to accept authorization requests (0100s) that have no financial impact. The full service issuer may choose to manage the cardholder's available balance or credit line by placing a temporary hold on funds until it receives the 0220 advice. Because there could be circumstances in which the issuer does not receive the 0220 advice (for instance, a reversal was not properly processed), the full service issuer may want to establish an expiration date for holds, possibly three to four days after the authorization date. Another consideration for full service issuers is that for cross-currency transactions from authorization-only acquirers, the cardholder billing amount in the 0220 message may be different from the amount authorized. This difference may be due to fluctuations in currency conversion rates between the date of the authorization and the date that the transaction clears. Full service issuers also need to remember that acquirers may not know the final amount at the time of authorization and that some transactions may not have required an authorization because they were below the floor limit.

text_a: Routing refers to sending messages between VisaNet and acquirer and issuer processing centers. Routing also refers to issuer-specified conditions triggering Visa stand-in processing (STIP) to authorize a transaction on an issuer's behalf.

Visa assumes responsibility for routing a request to its proper destination. For instance, acquirers do not have to determine the destination of their authorization or financial requests because V.I.P. routes requests based on the account number in the message. In some cases, V.I.P. uses data other than the account number to determine message routing. Issuers designate which of their issuer processing centers should receive the requests. The issuer associates each issuing identifier (a range of card numbers for a specific card program, such as Visa Classic) with a specific issuer processing center. Optionally, issuers can control which processing center receives requests for their cardholders by designating multiple processing centers and specifying the types of transactions VisaNet should route to each processing center. changes.old: There are three types of interchange reimbursement fees (IRFs). Domestic Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in the same country. Intraregional Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in different countries within the same Visa region. Interregional Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in different Visa regions. In this context, transaction country is the country in which the transaction takes place, and issuing country is the country of the issuer of the card used in the transaction. If no domestic IRF has been established, the intraregional IRF applies. If no intraregional IRF has been established, the interregional (international) IRF applies. IRFs are settled daily through the settlement process. For National Net Settlement Service transactions, there is only one settlement currency, so balancing does not involve currency conversion. For International Settlement Service transactions, however, there are many settlement currencies. Visa uses buy and sell rates for currency conversion. These rates are paired into USD-based rates used when converting non- USD currencies against the U.S. dollar, and cross-rates (non-USD-based rates) used for selected currencies in which the rates quoted are against a currency other than the U.S. dollar. The Multicurrency Service automatically converts the transaction currency to the acquirer's settlement currency (if the two are different), and automatically converts the cardholder's billing currency to the issuer's settlement currency (if the two are different), to one of the settlement currencies. For POS transactions, IRFs are typically paid by acquirers to issuers. Fees for manual cash disbursements, reversals, merchandise returns, dispute financials, and credit adjustments flow in the opposite direction. Participating acquirers get authorization information that can improve billing accuracy and reduce fraud and dispute losses. The file also provides accurate point-of-entry information, enabling acquirers to differentiate between a transaction originating from a manual key entry from one originating from a proximity payment terminal, and distinguish between a transaction made with a chip card containing a CVV from a transaction made with a chip card without a CVV. Raw data files—Recipients can use raw data files, in conjunction with VSS machine- readable reports, to automate the reconciliation process. As an optional service, Visa provides raw data files that contain detailed information about the settlement day's transactions for a given participant. Raw data is distinguished from report data in that it is suited for automated processing. The raw data records are produced from the same sources as SMS reports.
